title: Replay QA — Continuous QA
subtitle: Point it at your app; it explores, files bugs, and re-verifies your fixes.
throughline: one bug, from the exploration that discovers it to the journey retry that proves it fixed, looped from your agent and your CI.

chapters.title: The Autonomous Loop
chapters.blurb: Point Replay QA at a URL and it explores the app, builds journeys, and files bugs on its own.

story.title: The Autonomous Loop
story.subtitle: Point it at your app; it explores, files bugs, and re-verifies your fixes.

steps.title: The Autonomous Loop
steps.narration: **Replay QA** is a platform for autonomously testing and reporting bugs in web apps. You give it a URL; it does the rest.
steps.say: Point Replay QA at a running web app, and it tests that app for you, around the clock, with no human writing the tests.
steps.coverSubtitle: How one bug is discovered, reported, fixed, and re-verified.

steps.title: Create a project
steps.narration: You create a project with the app's `target_url` and free-text `instructions` — `POST /projects`. That single call kicks off the whole autonomous run.
steps.say: It starts with one thing you hand it: the address of the app you want tested. You create a project, giving Replay QA that target URL and a sentence of instructions.

steps.title: Agents explore the app
steps.narration: The service launches **explorations** — agents that drive the live app, probing auth, navigation, persistence, and UI. Each run is captured as a Replay recording.
steps.say: Replay QA spawns exploration agents that open the app and start clicking through it like a curious user, hunting for broken flows, bad validation, and visual regressions.

steps.title: A bug is filed
steps.narration: A discovered defect becomes a **bug** row — `createBug()` — always starting `status: open`, with repro steps, expected/actual behavior, and analysis.
steps.say: When an agent finds something wrong, it files a bug. Every new bug starts life with the status open, carrying reproduction steps, expected versus actual behavior, and a root cause analysis.

steps.title: Flows become journeys
steps.narration: Stable flows are promoted to **journeys** — saved, repeatable test scripts. `queueJourneyTasksForProject` later re-runs the eligible ones.
steps.say: The interesting flows it discovers get saved as journeys: repeatable test scripts that capture one path through your app, so the same scenario can be replayed again later.

steps.title: Journeys run as test runs
steps.narration: Each journey executes as a **test run** (`test_runs`); `countBugsForTestRun` drives the retry gate. Exploration widens coverage; journeys keep it honest over time.
steps.say: From then on, each journey runs as a test run against your app, and any test run can file fresh bugs of its own. That is the loop: explore, build journeys, run them, report.

steps.title: One URL, a standing QA system
steps.narration: The full loop: a `target_url` becomes **explorations** and **journeys** that continuously produce **bugs** — a self-sustaining QA system you point at an app and leave running.
steps.say: So one URL turns into a standing QA system: agents explore, journeys lock in coverage, bugs pile up with evidence, and the whole thing keeps running so regressions surface the moment they appear.

chapters.title: Plug In Your Agent
chapters.blurb: Install a Replay plugin bundle and your coding agent gets scripts that speak the Replay QA API.

story.title: Plug In Your Agent
story.subtitle: Point it at your app; it explores, files bugs, and re-verifies your fixes.

steps.title: Plug In Your Agent
steps.narration: The **plugins** repo is a registry of agent bundles. Installing one teaches your agent to run Replay QA for itself.
steps.say: Replay QA isn't a place you visit. It plugs straight into the coding agent you already use.
steps.coverSubtitle: Install a bundle; your agent gets scripts that speak the Replay QA API.

steps.title: Install a bundle
steps.narration: `npx shadcn add replayio/plugins/claude-code` drops a **replay-qa** skill into your repo — `SKILL.md` plus a folder of Node scripts. Bundles exist for Codex, Cursor, OpenCode too.
steps.say: The plugins repository is a registry of bundles, one per agent: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more. You install one with a single shadcn add command.

steps.title: Scripts, not raw endpoints
steps.narration: Commands like `full-qa.js` and `mark-bug.js` all call `apiRequest()` in `replay-qa-lib.js` — one HTTP helper, so the model never hand-rolls URLs.
steps.say: The skill teaches your agent to drive Replay QA through those scripts instead of memorizing raw endpoints. Each script funnels through one small library.

steps.title: Find the token
steps.narration: `getAuthToken()` reads `REPLAY_QA_API_KEY`, then `REPLAY_API_KEY` / `REPLAY_ACCESS_TOKEN`, then `~/.replay/profile/auth.json`. Tokens start with `lqa_` and ride as a Bearer header.
steps.say: Before any call goes out, the library finds your token. It checks a few environment variables, then falls back to the Replay login profile on disk.

steps.title: Remember the project
steps.narration: `ensureProject()` resolves the id from an argument, the environment, or `.replay/config.json`'s `qa-project-id` — and `writeConfigProjectId()` persists a freshly created one back.
steps.say: It also remembers which project this repo belongs to. The first run writes the project id into a small config file; every later run reuses it instead of creating a duplicate.

steps.title: Make the call
steps.narration: `apiRequest()` hits `https://qa.replay.io/api/v1` with the Bearer token — e.g. `GET /projects/:id/status` — and returns parsed JSON to the agent.
steps.say: With a token and a project in hand, the script makes its call: bearer authenticated HTTPS to the Replay QA API, and it hands the answer back to your agent.

steps.title: A thin, boring bridge
steps.narration: The bundle is the bridge: **skill** → **script** → `replay-qa-lib.js` → **Replay QA API**, with the **token** and **project id** resolved automatically on every call.
steps.say: So the whole bridge is thin and boring on purpose: your agent loads a skill, runs a script, the script authenticates and remembers the project, and Replay QA answers.

chapters.title: Fix, Mark, Re-verify
chapters.blurb: Pull the bug report, patch the code, mark it fixed, and let Replay QA re-run the affected journey.

story.title: Fix, Mark, Re-verify
story.subtitle: Point it at your app; it explores, files bugs, and re-verifies your fixes.

steps.title: Fix, Mark, Re-verify
steps.narration: The repair loop: surface a **bug**, patch the code, `mark-bug.js … fixed`, and let Replay QA re-run the journey to verify.
steps.say: Finding bugs is half the job. The real payoff is the tight loop where your agent fixes them and Replay QA proves the fix.
steps.coverSubtitle: Pull the report, patch the code, mark it fixed, let the journey re-run.

steps.title: Pull the open bugs
steps.narration: `full-qa.js` lists open bugs (`GET /projects/:id/bugs?status=open`), collects their ids, and fetches each detail with `GET /bugs/:id`.
steps.say: Your agent runs the full QA script, which pulls every open bug for the project, then fetches the detailed report behind each one.

steps.title: Read the report first
steps.narration: The **bug detail** carries repro steps, expected/actual behavior, severity, a linked Replay recording, and root-cause analysis — the primary debugging source, not source-reading guesses.
steps.say: Each report is the source of truth: reproduction steps, expected versus actual behavior, the captured evidence, and a root cause analysis. The agent reads all of it before touching code.

steps.title: Fix it in your codebase
steps.narration: The agent patches the code from the bug evidence plus the current source — grouping fixes by root cause and affected file before editing.
steps.say: Now the agent does the real work in your codebase: it edits the exact files the report points to, fixing the defect from the evidence rather than from guesswork.

steps.title: Mark it fixed
steps.narration: `mark-bug.js <bug-id> fixed` sends `PATCH /bugs/:id { status: 'fixed' }`. Valid statuses: `fixed`, `wontfix`, `invalid`, `reopened`.
steps.say: When the fix is in, the agent marks the bug fixed. That is a single patch call to the bug's status, and it is the signal Replay QA was waiting for.

steps.title: The journey re-runs itself
steps.narration: Resolving all bugs on a journey version triggers a retry (`journey-retry.ts`). There is no direct single-journey rerun endpoint; marking fixed is the supported trigger.
steps.say: Marking it fixed doesn't just close a ticket. Resolving the bugs on a journey makes Replay QA automatically re-run that journey to check your work, with no manual rerun button needed.

steps.title: Verified, or reopened
steps.narration: The retried **test run** re-checks the flow. A genuine fix sticks; a regression flips the bug back to `reopened` and the repair loop repeats.
steps.say: The journey runs again against your patched app. If the bug is truly gone, it stays resolved; if it resurfaces, Replay QA reopens it and the loop comes back around.

steps.title: The repair loop
steps.narration: The repair loop end to end: **full-qa** surfaces a bug → you patch → **mark-bug** fixed → **journey retry** verifies → resolved or **reopened**. Repeat until no open bugs remain.
steps.say: Pull the report, fix the code, mark it fixed, let Replay QA re-verify. That cycle is what turns a pile of bugs into a steadily greener test suite.

chapters.title: Wire It Into CI
chapters.blurb: Run the same Replay QA scripts from a GitHub workflow: cancel stale runs, re-test, mark fixes, explore.

story.title: Wire It Into CI
story.subtitle: Point it at your app; it explores, files bugs, and re-verifies your fixes.

steps.title: Wire It Into CI
steps.narration: The same `replay-qa` scripts run in a **GitHub Actions** job, so QA rides along with every commit instead of waiting for a human.
steps.say: Once your agent can run Replay QA from a script, you can hand the whole loop to your continuous integration pipeline.
steps.coverSubtitle: On every push: cancel the stale run, re-test, mark fixes, explore the new build.

steps.title: Every push starts a run
steps.narration: A GitHub Actions workflow keyed `on: push` starts a run for each commit. The job invokes the same `replay-qa` scripts your agent uses locally.
steps.say: The trigger is simple: every push to your branch starts a workflow run. That run is where all the Replay QA scripts will execute.

steps.title: Cancel stale runs
steps.narration: A GitHub Actions `concurrency` group keyed by branch with `cancel-in-progress: true` cancels any still-running QA workflow when a newer push lands — stale runs never finish against old code, and a reused project (one `qa-project-id`) isn't double-driven.
steps.say: Push again before the last run finishes, and you don't want two QA runs racing on stale code. A concurrency group cancels the in-flight run so only the newest commit gets tested.

steps.title: Map the secret
steps.narration: Map the CI secret to the script's env: `REPLAY_QA_API_KEY` from `SECRET_REPLAY_QA_API_KEY` (a `lqa_` bearer token). Never echo it.
steps.say: First the job needs credentials. It maps your stored Replay QA secret into the environment variable the scripts look for, without ever printing it.

steps.title: Re-test the commit
steps.narration: `node full-qa.js` runs in CI: it reuses the project from `.replay/config.json` and calls `GET /projects/:id/bugs?status=open` to gate the build on real findings.
steps.say: Then it runs the full QA script, exactly as your agent would, pulling the project's open bugs for this commit.

steps.title: Mark bugs done
steps.narration: CI marks a fixed bug from the build: `mark-bug.js <bug-id> fixed` → `PATCH /bugs/:id { status: 'fixed' }`, which triggers the journey retry server-side.
steps.say: When a commit closes a known issue, the pipeline marks that bug done automatically, the same single status patch the agent uses by hand.

steps.title: Explore the new build
steps.narration: Trigger fresh coverage: `start-exploration.js "..."` → `POST /projects/:id/explorations { prompt }` (optional `agent_count`, 1–10) against the new deploy.
steps.say: And to widen coverage on the freshly deployed build, the pipeline can kick off a new exploration, pointing the agents at whatever changed.

steps.title: QA on every commit
steps.narration: The CI loop: **push** → **workflow** (stale runs cancelled) → **scripts** with the **secret** → **Replay QA API**: re-test, `mark-bug` fixes, and `start-exploration` on each commit.
steps.say: Push, cancel the stale run, authenticate, re-test, mark the fixes, and explore the new build. Your QA loop now rides along with every commit, hands free.

chapters.title: Inside the Loop
chapters.blurb: Behind the API: a scheduler steals warm containers, binds each to one project, and records every run.

story.title: Inside the Loop
story.subtitle: Point it at your app; it explores, files bugs, and re-verifies your fixes.

steps.title: Inside the Loop
steps.narration: Under the REST surface: `tasks`, a warm container pool, and project-scoped dispatch — `netlify/functions/lib/tasks.ts`.
steps.say: Behind that simple API is a scheduler that spins up real browsers, one project at a time, and keeps them strictly isolated.
steps.coverSubtitle: How a queued task becomes a recorded run — and why each container serves one project for life.

steps.title: Work is queued
steps.narration: `createTask()` enqueues work in `tasks`; every work-creating call site then calls `triggerSpawnForProject(projectId)` — `spawn-workers-background` is the only spawner.
steps.say: Every piece of work — a test run, an exploration, a polish pass — first becomes a queued task. Creating that task fires a spawn request for just that project.

steps.title: Steal from the warm pool
steps.narration: `spawn-workers-background` either `stealPoolContainer(projectId)` from the warm pool (size `POOL_SIZE`, 6) or spawns a new Fly worker — then tops the pool back up.
steps.say: To avoid cold start latency, a global pool of pre-warmed containers sits idle. The spawner steals one and wakes it instantly, or spins up a fresh machine if the pool is empty.

steps.title: One project for life
steps.narration: Allocation sets `app_containers.project_id` once, for life (`pool` → `worker`). The single-project invariant prevents cross-project recording, auth, and session contamination.
steps.say: The moment a container is allocated, it is bound to one project for the rest of its life. It is never handed to a different project, and that isolation stops one tenant's recording from leaking into another's bug.

steps.title: Project-scoped dispatch
steps.narration: `claimNextTask(containerName)` is strictly project-scoped — it returns only queued tasks whose `project_id` matches the container's binding, using `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.
steps.say: The bound container polls for work, and the dispatcher only ever hands it tasks for its own project. An unbound pool container polls but claims nothing.

steps.title: Drive and record
steps.narration: `container-task-webhook` builds the prompt (`buildQAPrompt` / `buildExplorationPrompt`); the run drives the app and captures a Replay recording at `app.replay.io/recording/...`.
steps.say: Now it does the real testing: it drives your app through the task's journey or exploration, and records the entire browser session as a Replay recording.

steps.title: File the bug with evidence
steps.narration: Findings are written as **bugs** with the run's `replay_recording_id` attached; an unusable recording is dropped so a bug never links a dead recording.
steps.say: Anything broken becomes a bug, with that recording attached, so when you open the report you can watch the exact session that produced it.

steps.title: The engine that keeps turning
steps.narration: The whole engine: **task** → **spawn** steals a warm **container** (one project for life) → drives the **app**, saves a **recording**, files **bugs**, and re-queues on resolve (`journey-retry.ts`).
steps.say: A task queues, a warm container is bound to one project, it drives your app and records it, files bugs, and retires clean. That is the engine that makes continuous QA actually continuous.
